stem: A 24-year-old known asthmatic patient presents to the emergency department with sudden worsening shortness of breath, diffuse wheeze, and chest tightness for the past 2 hours. Peak expiratory flow rate (PEF) is significantly reduced compared to baseline. There is no fever, no productive cough, and no history of allergen exposure or rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?

keywords: Known asthmatic patient → Strong baseline risk for asthma flare
Sudden worsening dyspnea + diffuse wheeze + ↓ PEF → Classic acute bronchial obstruction pattern (asthma exacerbation triad)
No fever, no productive cough, no rash/exposure history → Rules out infection and allergic systemic causes

1. Known asthmatic patient → Strong baseline risk for asthma flare
  2. Sudden worsening dyspnea + diffuse wheeze + ↓ PEF → Classic acute bronchial obstruction pattern (asthma exacerbation triad)
  3. No fever, no productive cough, no rash/exposure history → Rules out infection and allergic systemic causes

C.title: Acute asthma exacerbation
C.body: A known asthmatic presenting with sudden onset respiratory distress strongly suggests an acute exacerbation of underlying airway hyperreactivity. The key physiological event is reversible bronchoconstriction with airflow limitation, reflected by reduced PEF. Absence of fever or sputum further supports a non-infective inflammatory airway process. This is the most direct and high-yield diagnosis in this clinical setting.
C.bodyHtml: A known asthmatic presenting with sudden onset respiratory distress strongly suggests an acute exacerbation of underlying airway hyperreactivity. The key physiological event is reversible bronchoconstriction with airflow limitation, reflected by reduced PEF. Absence of fever or sputum further supports a non-infective inflammatory airway process. This is the most direct and high-yield diagnosis in this clinical setting.
C.clinicalReasoning: This condition occurs due to airway inflammation, bronchial smooth muscle constriction, and mucus plugging. Patients present with episodic dyspnea, wheeze, and chest tightness. PEF reduction is a sensitive marker of severity and response to treatment. In a known asthmatic, sudden deterioration without infection strongly favors exacerbation over alternative diagnoses.

A.title: Acute COPD exacerbation
A.body: COPD exacerbation refers to acute worsening of chronic airflow limitation, usually in older patients with a smoking history. It typically presents with increased dyspnea, sputum production, and sometimes infection-triggered symptoms. Wheeze may be present but is less reversible compared to asthma. Age and history are key distinguishing factors.
A.bodyHtml: COPD exacerbation refers to acute worsening of chronic airflow limitation, usually in older patients with a smoking history. It typically presents with increased dyspnea, sputum production, and sometimes infection-triggered symptoms. Wheeze may be present but is less reversible compared to asthma. Age and history are key distinguishing factors.
A.clinicalReasoning: This patient is young (24 years) with no COPD risk profile, making this diagnosis unlikely. COPD is characterized by progressive, non-reversible airflow limitation. Exacerbations are usually triggered by infection or pollutants. Absence of chronic symptoms or risk factors strongly argues against COPD.

Exacerbations are usually triggered by infection or pollutants. Absence of chronic symptoms or risk factors strongly argues against COPD.

B.title: Acute bronchitis
B.body: Acute bronchitis is an inflammatory condition of the tracheobronchial tree, usually viral in origin. It presents with cough (often productive), mild dyspnea, and sometimes wheeze. Fever may or may not be present. It is typically self-limiting.
B.bodyHtml: Acute bronchitis is an inflammatory condition of the tracheobronchial tree, usually viral in origin. It presents with cough (often productive), mild dyspnea, and sometimes wheeze. Fever may or may not be present. It is typically self-limiting.
B.clinicalReasoning: Although bronchitis can cause wheeze, the hallmark is persistent cough rather than severe airflow limitation. A marked reduction in PEF is not typical. The acute bronchospasm severity in this case exceeds simple bronchitis. Lack of cough also makes this option unlikely.

D.title: Pneumothorax
D.body: Pneumothorax is caused by air entry into pleural space leading to lung collapse. It presents with sudden unilateral chest pain and dyspnea, with reduced or absent breath sounds on one side. Tracheal deviation may occur in tension pneumothorax.

D.clinicalReasoning: This case describes diffuse wheeze rather than unilateral absent breath sounds. Pneumothorax does not typically cause diffuse wheeze or reduced PEF pattern seen in asthma. There is also no mention of pleuritic chest pain or asymmetry. Thus, this diagnosis is less likely.

E.title: Vocal cord dysfunction
E.body: Vocal cord dysfunction involves paradoxical vocal cord closure during inspiration, mimicking asthma. It presents with episodic dyspnea and inspiratory stridor rather than expiratory wheeze. It is often misdiagnosed as asthma but does not show bronchodilator-responsive airflow obstruction.
E.bodyHtml: Vocal cord dysfunction involves paradoxical vocal cord closure during inspiration, mimicking asthma. It presents with episodic dyspnea and inspiratory stridor rather than expiratory wheeze. It is often misdiagnosed as asthma but does not show bronchodilator-responsive airflow obstruction.
E.clinicalReasoning: This condition typically shows normal PEF or variable inspiratory flow limitation rather than significant bronchial obstruction. Absence of wheeze pattern and presence of inspiratory noise differentiate it from asthma. Known asthma history and objective PEF reduction strongly favor asthma exacerbation instead.

keyConcept: Acute asthma exacerbation is diagnosed in a known asthmatic patient who presents with sudden onset dyspnea, diffuse wheeze, and reduced peak expiratory flow rate, especially in the absence of infective or systemic allergic features. The key discriminator is reversible airway obstruction demonstrated by decreased PEF in a typical clinical context.

diagram.description: This diagram illustrates the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and diagnostic evaluation of acute asthma exacerbation. It compares a normal airway with an asthmatic airway during an attack, highlighting bronchial smooth muscle constriction, mucosal edema, and mucus plugging leading to reversible airflow obstruction. The figure also summarizes common triggers, key clinical features, severity assessment using peak expiratory flow (PEF), and important diagnostic indicators used in emergency and internal medicine practice.
